Que.q: Q1 : what is React?
Que.a: React is an open-source front-end JavaScript library that is used for building user interfaces, especially for single-page applications. It is used for handling view layer for web and mobile apps. React was created by Jordan Walke, a software engineer working for Facebook. React was first deployed on Facebook's News Feed in 2011 and on Instagram in 2012.

Que.q: Q2 : How does React work?
Que.a: React creates a virtual DOM. When state changes in a component it firstly runs a 'diffing' algorithm, which identifies what has changed in the virtual DOM. The second step is reconciliation, where it updates the DOM with the results of the difference

Que.q: Q3 : What are the major features of React?
Que.a: The major features of React are:

list.1: It uses VirtualDOM instead of RealDOM considering that RealDOM manipulations are expensive.
list.2: Supports server-side rendering.
list.3: Follows Unidirectional data flow or data binding.
list.4: Uses reusable/composable UI components to develop the view.

Que.q: Q5 : What is the virtual DOM?
Que.a: The virtual DOM (VDOM) is a programming concept where an ideal, or “virtual”, representation of a UI is kept in memory and synced with the “real” DOM by a library such as ReactDOM. This process is called reconciliation.This approach enables the declarative API of React: You tell React what state you want the UI to be in, and it makes sure the DOM matches that state. This abstracts out the attribute manipulation, event handling, and manual DOM updating that you would otherwise have to use to build your app.

Que.q: Q6 : Is the Shadow DOM the same as the Virtual DOM?
Que.a: No, they are different. The Shadow DOM is a browser technology designed primarily for scoping variables and CSS in web components. The virtual DOM is a concept implemented by libraries in JavaScript on top of browser APIs.

list.1: Web browsers cannot read JSX directly. This is because they are built to only read regular JS objects and JSX is not a regular JavaScript object.
list.2: For a web browser to read a JSX file, the file needs to be transformed into a regular JavaScript object. For this, we use Babel.

Que.q: Q11 : When to use a Class Component over a Function Component?
Que.a: If the component needs state or lifecycle methods then use class component otherwise use function component. However, from React 16.8 with the addition of Hooks, you could use state , lifecycle methods and other features that were only available in class component right in your function component. *So, it is always recommended to use Function components, unless you need a React functionality whose Function component equivalent is not present yet, like Error Boundaries *

Que.q: Q12 : What are Pure Components?
Que.a: React.PureComponent is exactly the same as React.Component except that it handles the shouldComponentUpdate() method for you. When props or state changes, PureComponent will do a shallow comparison on both props and state. Component on the other hand won't compare current props and state to next out of the box. Thus, the component will re-render by default whenever shouldComponentUpdate is called.

Que.q: Q13 : What is state in React?
Que.a: State of a component is an object that holds some information that may change over the lifetime of the component. We should always try to make our state as simple as possible and minimize the number of stateful components.

Que.q: Q14 : What are props in React?
Que.a: Props are inputs to components. They are single values or objects containing a set of values that are passed to components on creation using a naming convention similar to HTML-tag attributes. They are data passed down from a parent component to a child component.

Que.list_text: The primary purpose of props in React is to provide following component functionality:

list.1: Pass custom data to your component.
list.2: Trigger state changes.
list.3: Use via this.props.reactProp inside component's render() method.

Que.q: Q15 : What is the difference between state and props?
Que.a: Both props and state are plain JavaScript objects. While both of them hold information that influences the output of render, they are different in their functionality with respect to component. Props get passed to the component similar to function parameters whereas state is managed within the component similar to variables declared within a function.

Que.q: Q16 : Why should we not update the state directly?

Que.simple_text: If you try to update the state directly then it won't re-render the component.
Que.code:
//Wrong

Que.simple_text: Instead use setState() method. It schedules an update to a component's state object. When state changes, the component responds by re-rendering.
Que.code:
//Correct
this.setState({ message: 'Hello World' })

Que.note: Note: You can directly assign to the state object either in constructor or using latest javascript's class field declaration syntax.

Que.q: Q17 : What is the purpose of callback function as an argument of setState()?
Que.a: The callback function is invoked when setState finished and the component gets rendered. Since setState() is asynchronous the callback function is used for any post action.

Que.code: setState({ name: 'John' }, () => console.log('The name has updated and component re-rendered'))

Que.note: Note: It is recommended to use lifecycle method rather than this callback function.

Que.a: Refs provide a way to access DOM nodes or React elements created in the render method. They should be avoided in most cases, however, they can be useful when we need direct access to the DOM element or an instance of a component.

list.2: Triggering imperative animations.

Que.q: Q25 : How Virtual DOM works?
Que.a: The Virtual DOM works in three simple steps.

list.1: Whenever any underlying data changes, the entire UI is re-rendered in Virtual DOM representation.

list.2: Then the difference between the previous DOM representation and the new one is calculated.

list.3: Once the calculations are done, the real DOM will be updated with only the things that have actually changed.

Que.q: Q26 : What is React Fiber?
Que.a: Fiber is the new reconciliation engine or reimplementation of core algorithm in React v16. The goal of React Fiber is to increase its suitability for areas like animation, layout, gestures, ability to pause, abort, or reuse work and assign priority to different types of updates; and new concurrency primitives.

Que.q: Q27 : What is the main goal of React Fiber?
Que.a: The goal of React Fiber is to increase its suitability for areas like animation, layout, and gestures. Its headline feature is incremental rendering: the ability to split rendering work into chunks and spread it out over multiple frames.

list.1: Ability to split interruptible work in chunks.
list.2: Ability to prioritize, rebase and reuse work in progress.
list.3: Ability to split interruptible work in chunks.Ability to yield back and forth between parents and children to support layout in React.
list.4: Ability to return multiple elements from render().

Que.q: Q31 : What is Lifting State Up in React?
Que.a: When several components need to share the same changing data then it is recommended to lift the shared state up to their closest common ancestor. That means if two child components share the same data from its parent, then move the state to parent instead of maintaining local state in both of the child components.

Que.q: Q32 : What are the different phases of component lifecycle?
Que.a: The component lifecycle has three distinct lifecycle phases:

list.Mounting: The component is ready to mount in the browser DOM. This phase covers initialization from constructor(), getDerivedStateFromProps(), render(), and componentDidMount() lifecycle methods.
list.Updating: In this phase, the component gets updated in two ways, sending the new props and updating the state either from setState() or forceUpdate(). This phase covers getDerivedStateFromProps(), shouldComponentUpdate(), render(), getSnapshotBeforeUpdate() and componentDidUpdate() lifecycle methods.
list.Unmounting: In this last phase, the component is not needed and gets unmounted from the browser DOM. This phase includes componentWillUnmount() lifecycle method.

list.Updating: Pre-commit Before the component actually applies the changes to the DOM, there is a moment that allows React to read from the DOM through the getSnapshotBeforeUpdate().
list.Unmounting: Commit React works with the DOM and executes the final lifecycles respectively componentDidMount() for mounting, componentDidUpdate() for updating, and componentWillUnmount() for unmounting.

Que.q: Q33 : What are the lifecycle methods of React?

list.componentWillMount: Executed before rendering and is used for App level configuration in your root component.
list.componentDidMount: Executed after first rendering and here all AJAX requests, DOM or state updates, and set up event listeners should occur.
list.componentWillReceiveProps: Executed when particular prop updates to trigger state transitions.
list.shouldComponentUpdate: Determines if the component will be updated or not. By default it returns true. If you are sure that the component doesn't need to render after state or props are updated, you can return false value. It is a great place to improve performance as it allows you to prevent a re-render if component receives new prop.
list.componentWillUpdate: Executed before re-rendering the component when there are props & state changes confirmed by shouldComponentUpdate() which returns true.
list.componentDidUpdate: Mostly it is used to update the DOM in response to prop or state changes.
list.componentWillUnmount: It will be used to cancel any outgoing network requests, or remove all event listeners associated with the component.

list.getDerivedStateFromProps: Invoked right before calling render() and is invoked on every render. This exists for rare use cases where you need a derived state. Worth reading if you need derived state.
list.componentDidMount: Executed after first rendering and where all AJAX requests, DOM or state updates, and set up event listeners should occur.
list.shouldComponentUpdate: Determines if the component will be updated or not. By default, it returns true. If you are sure that the component doesn't need to render after the state or props are updated, you can return a false value. It is a great place to improve performance as it allows you to prevent a re-render if component receives a new prop.
list.getSnapshotBeforeUpdate: : Executed right before rendered output is committed to the DOM. Any value returned by this will be passed into componentDidUpdate(). This is useful to capture information from the DOM i.e. scroll position.
list.componentDidUpdate: Mostly it is used to update the DOM in response to prop or state changes. This will not fire if shouldComponentUpdate() returns false
list.componentWillUnmount: It will be used to cancel any outgoing network requests, or remove all event listeners associated with the component.

Que.a: When a component's props or state change, React decides whether an actual DOM update is necessary by comparing the newly returned element with the previously rendered one. When they are not equal, React will update the DOM. This process is called reconciliation.

Que.q: Q43 : Why fragments are better than container divs?
Que.a: Below are the list of reasons,

Que.q: Q45 : What are stateless components?
Que.a: If the behaviour of a component is independent of its state then it can be a stateless component. You can use either a function or a class for creating stateless components. But unless you need to use a lifecycle hook in your components, you should go for function components. There are a lot of benefits if you decide to use function components here; they are easy to write, understand, and test, a little faster, and you can avoid the this keyword altogether.

Que.q: Q46 : What are stateful components?
Que.a: If the behaviour of a component is dependent on the state of the component then it can be termed as stateful component. These stateful components are always class components and have a state that gets initialized in the constructor.

Que.simple_text: Hooks let you use state and other React features without writing classes.

Que.a: Below are the list of main advantages of React,

list.1: Increases the application's performance with Virtual DOM.
list.2: JSX makes code easy to read and write.
list.3: It renders both on client and server side (SSR)
list.4: Easy to integrate with frameworks (Angular, Backbone) since it is only a view library.
list.5: Easy to write unit and integration tests with tools such as Jest.

Que.a: Apart from the advantages, there are few limitations of React too,

list.1: React is just a view library, not a full framework.
list.2: There is a learning curve for beginners who are new to web development.
list.3: Integrating React into a traditional MVC framework requires some additional configuration.
list.4: The code complexity increases with inline templating and JSX.

Que.q: Q55 : What is prop drilling in React?
Que.a: Props drilling is the process of passing data or props from a parent component to a child component. But, in between, other components have access to the data or props as we are passing it down the chain. This would result in unnecessary exchange of data to the component which don't really need it. To avoid this we can use possible solutions like React context API, Redux etc.

Que.note: The disadvantage of using prop drilling is that the components that should otherwise be not aware of the data have access to the data.

Que.q: Q56 : What is React Hooks?
Que.a: React Hooks are the built-in functions that permit developers for using the state and lifecycle methods within React components. These are newly added features made available in React 16.8 version. Each lifecycle of a component is having 3 phases which include mount, unmount, and update. Along with that, components have properties and states. Hooks will allow using these methods by developers for improving the reuse of code with higher flexibility navigating the component tree.Using Hook, all features of React can be used without writing class components. For example, before React version 16.8, it required a class component for managing the state of a component. But now using the useState hook, we can keep the state in a functional component.

Que.q: Q57 : What are Hooks?
Que.a: Hooks are functions that let us “hook into” React state and lifecycle features from a functional component.React Hooks cannot be used in class components. They let us write components without class.

Que.q: Q58 : What rules need to be followed for hooks?
Que.a: You need to follow two rules in order to use hooks,

list.1: Call Hooks only at the top level of your react functions. i.e, You shouldn’t call Hooks inside loops, conditions, or nested functions. This will ensure that Hooks are called in the same order each time a component renders and it preserves the state of Hooks between multiple useState and useEffect calls.
list.2: Call Hooks from React Functions only. i.e, You shouldn’t call Hooks from regular JavaScript functions.

Que.q: Q75 : What is flux?
Que.a: Flux is an application design paradigm used as a replacement for the more traditional MVC pattern. It is not a framework or a library but a new kind of architecture that complements React and the concept of Unidirectional Data Flow. Facebook uses this pattern internally when working with React.

Que.q: Q76 : What is Redux?
Que.a: Redux is a predictable state container for JavaScript apps based on the Flux design pattern. Redux can be used together with React, or with any other view library. It is tiny (about 2kB) and has no dependencies.

Que.q: Q77 : What are the core principles of Redux?
Que.a: Redux follows three fundamental principles:

list.Single source of truth: The state of your whole application is stored in an object tree within a single store. The single state tree makes it easier to keep track of changes over time and debug or inspect the application.
list.State is read-only: The only way to change the state is to emit an action, an object describing what happened. This ensures that neither the views nor the network callbacks will ever write directly to the state.
list.hanges are made with pure functions: To specify how the state tree is transformed by actions, you write reducers. Reducers are just pure functions that take the previous state and an action as parameters, and return the next state.

Que.q: Q78 : What are the downsides of Redux compared to Flux?
Que.a: Instead of saying downsides we can say that there are few compromises of using Redux over Flux. Those are as follows:

list.You will need to learn to avoid mutation: Flux is un-opinionated about mutating data, but Redux doesn't like mutations and many packages complementary to Redux assume you never mutate the state. You can enforce this with dev-only packages like redux-immutable-state-invariant, Immutable.js, or instructing your team to write non-mutating code.
list.You're going to have to carefully pick y: While Flux explicitly doesn't try to solve problems such as undo/redo, persistence, or forms, Redux has extension points such as middleware and store enhancers, and it has spawned a rich ecosystem.
list.There is no nice Flow integration yet: Flux currently lets you do very impressive static type checks which Redux doesn't support yet.

list.1: DOM manipulation is very expensive which causes applications to behave slow and inefficient.
list.2: Due to circular dependencies, a complicated model was created around models and views.
list.3: Lot of data changes happens for collaborative applications(like Google Docs).
list.4: No way to do undo (travel back in time) easily without adding so much extra code.

Que.q: Q80 : Are there any similarities between Redux and RxJS?
Que.a: These libraries are very different for very different purposes, but there are some vague similarities. Redux is a tool for managing state throughout the application. It is usually used as an architecture for UIs. Think of it as an alternative to (half of) Angular. RxJS is a reactive programming library. It is usually used as a tool to accomplish asynchronous tasks in JavaScript. Think of it as an alternative to Promises. Redux uses the Reactive paradigm because the Store is reactive. The Store observes actions from a distance, and changes itself. RxJS also uses the Reactive paradigm, but instead of being an architecture, it gives you basic building blocks, Observables, to accomplish this pattern.

Que.q: Q81 : What is the difference between React context and React Redux?
Que.a: You can use Context in your application directly and is going to be great for passing down data to deeply nested components which what it was designed for. Whereas Redux is much more powerful and provides a large number of features that the Context API doesn't provide. Also, React Redux uses context internally but it doesn't expose this fact in the public API.

Que.q: Q82 : Should I keep all component's state in Redux store?
Que.a: Keep your data in the Redux store, and the UI related state internally in the component.

Que.q: Q83 : What is the difference between component and container in React Redux?
Que.a: Component is a class or function component that describes the presentational part of your application. Container is an informal term for a component that is connected to a Redux store. Containers subscribe to Redux state updates and dispatch actions, and they usually don't render DOM elements; they delegate rendering to presentational child components.

Que.q: Q84 : How to structure Redux top level directories?
Que.a: Most of the applications has several top-level directories as below:

list.Components: Used for dumb components unaware of Redux.
list.Containers: Used for smart components connected to Redux.
list.Actions: Used for all action creators, where file names correspond to part of the app.
list.Reducers: Used for all reducers, where files name correspond to state key.

Que.a: redux-saga is a library that aims to make side effects (asynchronous things like data fetching and impure things like accessing the browser cache) in React/Redux applications easier and better.

Que.code: $ npm install --save redux-saga

Que.q: Q86 : What is the mental model of redux-saga?
Que.a: Saga is like a separate thread in your application, that's solely responsible for side effects. redux-saga is a redux middleware, which means this thread can be started, paused and cancelled from the main application with normal Redux actions, it has access to the full Redux application state and it can dispatch Redux actions as well.

Que.q: Q87 : What is Redux Thunk?
Que.a: Redux Thunk middleware allows you to write action creators that return a function instead of an action. The thunk can be used to delay the dispatch of an action, or to dispatch only if a certain condition is met. The inner function receives the store methods dispatch() and getState() as parameters.

Que.q: Q88 : What are the differences between redux-saga and redux-thunk?
Que.a: Both Redux Thunk and Redux Saga take care of dealing with side effects. In most of the scenarios, Thunk uses Promises to deal with them, whereas Saga uses Generators. Thunk is simple to use and Promises are familiar to many developers, Sagas/Generators are more powerful but you will need to learn them. But both middleware can coexist, so you can start with Thunks and introduce Sagas when/if you need them.

Que.q: Q93 : What is render hijacking in react?
Que.a: The concept of render hijacking is the ability to control what a component will output from another component. It means that you decorate your component by wrapping it into a Higher-Order component. By wrapping, you can inject additional props or make other changes, which can cause changing logic of rendering. It does not actually enable hijacking, but by using HOC you make your component behave differently

Que.q: Q94 : What are HOC factory implementations?
Que.a: There are two main ways of implementing HOCs in React.

list.1: Props Proxy (PP) and
list.2: Inheritance Inversion (II).

Que.simple_text: In this approach, the render method of the HOC returns a React Element of the type of the WrappedComponent. We also pass through the props that the HOC receives, hence the name Props Proxy.

In this approach, the returned HOC class (Enhancer) extends the WrappedComponent. It is called Inheritance Inversion because instead of the WrappedComponent extending some Enhancer class, it is passively extended by the Enhancer. In this way the relationship between them seems inverse.

Que.q: Q95 : What is React lazy function?
Que.a: The React.lazy function lets you render a dynamic import as a regular component. It will automatically load the bundle containing the OtherComponent when the component gets rendered. This must return a Promise which resolves to a module with a default export containing a React component.

Que.note: Note: React.lazy and Suspense is not yet available for server-side rendering. If you want to do code-splitting in a server rendered app, we still recommend React Loadable.

Que.q: Q96 : What is React memo function?
